turns.text: Welcome to the interview.
Morning. Ready when you are.
What time did you go to bed last night?
Around eleven. Fairly reliable for me.
Thanks. Approximately how many hours did you sleep last night, and would you say you slept well? Why or why not?
About seven hours, give or take. I'd call it decent — I was up around 3:30 like usual, but that's routine for me at this point, not something that ruins the night.
What was the last activity you engaged in before going to bed, and why did you choose to do that activity?
Read on my phone, honestly — that crossword's mostly for the middle of the night. Before bed I just check the weather for whatever job's on tap next morning.
Got it, thanks for explaining. Over the past two weeks, what factors have most affected your sleep quality?

Over the past two weeks? Not much has changed, honestly — same routine, same 3:30 wake-up. If anything, a couple of noisier nights when a neighbor's dog got going, but nothing that really moved the needle for me.
Is that pretty typical for you, or has something about your sleep or routine changed recently?
Typical, yeah. Been like this for years now — my body just does its own thing at 3:30, and I've made my peace with it.
Overall, are you happy with how you are sleeping these days? Why or why not?
Yeah, more or less. It's not perfect sleep, but I get enough of it and I don't feel wrecked during the day, so I'm not going to lose sleep over losing sleep, so to speak.
You’ve probably heard the advice that adults should get 7–9 hours of sleep a night. Does that feel practical for you right now?

(3-4 sentences, right? I hear it.) Sounds nice on paper. In practice I get about seven, with a break in the middle, and that's just how the math works out for me — I'm not going to lie awake chasing an extra hour to hit some number.
What makes it easy or difficult for you to actually get that much sleep?

"Nothing fancy — same time every night helps, and not having to be anywhere at a set hour anymore takes the pressure off. What makes it harder is if a job runs late or the phone rings for an emergency call, that throws the whole evening off."
Many people check their mobile phones, tablets, or computers right before bed. Do you do this, too? Why or why not?
Nah, not really — my phone stays on the charger across the room once I'm winding down. Old habit, I guess, or maybe just not wanting one more screen after a day of squinting at lock mechanisms.
Thanks for explaining. Do you regularly use social media? If yes, how do you typically use it, especially in the hours before bed?
Not really, no — I look at it now and then during the day, but by evening I'd rather do the crossword than scroll through somebody's vacation photos.

Thanks, that makes sense. Now a quick question about technology in general: Do you regularly use AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or similar applications? If yes, what do you mainly use them for?

"Nah, I've poked at one once or twice when my daughter showed me — mostly just to see what the fuss was about. Didn't stick, though. I'd rather call someone who actually knows locks than type at a screen about it."

Thanks, that’s clear. Since you don’t really use social media or AI chatbots regularly, I’ll skip ahead a bit.

If you could improve one thing about your sleeping habits, what would it be?
Something small — sleeping through the night without that 3:30 wake-up would be nice, but honestly, it's not costing me sleep, just costing me the crossword's cleanest section.
Given your work, studies, or daily responsibilities, do you think that kind of change—sleeping straight through without the 3:30 wake-up—would be doable? Why or why not?

Ah yeah, it'd be doable. No boss clocking me in, no fixed shift — if I wanted to chase a fix, I could try shifting bedtime or cutting something out. But truth is I've never really tried, because it doesn't bother me enough to bother with it.

Thanks, that’s helpful to know.

Now a few quick background questions. Feel free to skip anything you’d rather not share:

What is your age, your profession, your country of birth, your current country of residence, and—if it’s different—when did you move?
58, locksmith — semi-retired now, but still locksmith. Born and raised right here, never left, so no move to speak of.

Thank you for sharing that. Those were all the main questions I had.

Before we wrap up, is there anything else about your sleep or bedtime routine that you think is important and hasn’t come up yet?
